clusters.name: Your grandfather Gordon's death, 1991–1994
clusters.reason: Around your grandfather Gordon dying in June 1991, within three years: your wrist injury stopped your playing and your anxiety climbed in late 1991; you and Rafe had a blow-up and he moved out; you were on your own, getting high, absorbed in fixing radios; by early 1992 you were lost and low, unable to get going, with your grandfather gone and your mother about to remarry. Your grandmother Winifred was treated for a thyroid tumour within a year of being widowed. You were bleak at community college through 1992, nights out playing pool, days asleep. Your mother married Desmond in October 1992. By early 1994 you were stung that your dad had never heard of the film you were making, and you found your drive again with an exchange in Lisbon and Porto. The shifts pile up steep and close in the months after the death and through the two years after, then settle as you raced through the rest of your degree.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Winifred's death, 2001–2004
clusters.reason: Around your grandmother Winifred dying in February 2004, within three years before: in September 2001 you were running out of steam for performing and your anxiety climbed; you were found to have bowel cancer in 2001 or 2002; in early 2002 you had a disastrous audition for the national orchestra and were done with performing, casting about for what came next. You were on poor terms with family and friends; you left Thornbury for Gull Harbour in September 2002, met Marisol at a winter party in early 2003, left Gull Harbour to live with her in Fenwick by June 2003, then split up within the year. You sank into a deep depression once you split, and it took hold that winter once you were back in Thornbury; at the bottom, minding a house near Hamish, you hardly moved from the sofa. You could not face your family, though you relied, gingerly, on friends Corbin, Dale and Silas. By January 2004 you began swimming laps, requested help from your parents with therapy costs, and returned to your therapist Victor Halloran; the gradual recovery started there. Your grandmother spent her final months in a back bedroom at your parents' home and died in February 2004. The shifts pile up steep and close around the years of her illness and your burnout, with your depression deepening as she declined, and settle as you returned to therapy and began to recover.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Lorna's death, 2008
clusters.reason: Around your grandmother Lorna dying in January 2008, within months: you were at Alder Creek building with Silas in July 2008, too drained for conversation with your mother; she pressed to visit you, your anxiety climbed, and you kept the door shut on her; the visit went wrong and she never got inside. You left for nursing school at Marlow Sound in September 2008 and stopped speaking to your mother; the silence held for roughly a year. Your aunt Imogen had a stroke with months of rehabilitation in January 2009. The shifts pile up around your grandmother's death and the months after, as you moved away to nursing school and cut contact with your mother, then settle as the year of silence ran its course.

clusters.name: Your marriage to Wren, 2017–2019
clusters.reason: Around your marriage to Wren in March 2017, within two and a half years: you saw your mother a bit less once Wren came along; your cousin Bella was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in her forties in October 2017; your sister Tara married James and had a baby on the way by October 2019; your aunt Imogen's memory was slipping and getting worse, and she lashed out when muddled. Your job steadied and paid well by June 2019, with far less strain, but your anxiety climbed in October 2019 as you constantly felt you ought to be driving your projects forward; you started a sleeping pill though sleep itself was no better. You aimed for shorter, more regular calls with your mother. In late October 2019 Wren was swamped, one thing after another—a street party, a fundraising dinner, then the drive to the lake for her mother's retirement party. You were too strict laying out a plan to settle her when she was swamped; she talks with her father and brother all day and nothing happens to one that the others don't hear. She settled once the weekend had a plan and the dinner went well, but you were awake from the small hours at the lake weekend with no more sleep, and could only pull back as the others rose; your sleep is at its worst around her family and you feel you don't belong. She was anxious when you'd had no sleep at family occasions, with long quiet drives home afterward. The shifts pile up in the months around the wedding and intensify in late 2019 as Wren's family gathered and your sleep broke down around them.
